items.title: Frank Wess — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Then Michael Weiss is doing half of the week; he’s usually with me. I’ve done a lot of things with Michael.

ctx.x: I have the players right here. You have Ted Nash, can you mention all the players.

Yeah, Ted Nash, Scott Robinson, Frank Greene, myself, Winard Harper on drums, and Peter Washington is doing part of the week and then I have Noreko, she’s a female Japanese bass player who plays with Diva. Then Michael Weiss is doing half of the week; he’s usually with me. I’ve done a lot of things with Michael. The last three days Tomoko Ohno is going to play with me, she’s worked with me before. I’ve taken her on gigs with me up in Connecticut and around. She’s a very good player; they’re both very good.

items.title: Michael Weiss interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 22, 2021
items.q: And you know to be able to play with somebody like that first-hand and experience that is priceless.

ctx.x: The stylistic changes in that hundred years are quite amazing and I’m wondering if it becomes harder and harder to be innovative and still create music that is listenable and appealing?

You know it’s all up to the music maker, what choices they make. You know I mean we were talking about what you were asking me about before — the last of the truth — I think what came to mind is like the way Frank Wess plays a phrase on his horn. He’s expressing his life experience. My experience and someone in their 30s or in their 20s can’t possibly have that experience to be able to express that way on their horn, what he heard, what he grew up with, what’s in his DNA. That’s what I’m talking about. And you…

Yeah I was wondering if you had words for — I have this little scenario in my head, you’re playing a gig with Frank Wess in a club in New York and it went well. And on the way home what are you feeling inside after that experience?
